title: Reading the report - and not over-reading it

questions.prompt: Why is the report never the source of truth in this repo?
options: Because the Markdown format loses precision
Because the report is written before the run finishes
Because the report is generated by a separate tool that may be out of date
Because report.py contains no measurement at all - it formats what metrics.py and the runner produced - so the raw runs/<run_id>.jsonl is what a reader must open to check a number
questions.explain: The derivation order is raw -> meta -> report. run_report(result) only formats the RunResult it is handed; every number in the .md was computed by metrics.py or by the runner. So the report can be wrong in two ways - bad data or bad formatting - and the only way to know is to recompute from the raw file. Markdown does not lose precision (the .md prints values rounded for humans, and the JSONL keeps them). The report is written after the run completes, by the same code, in the same process - there is no separate tool and no staleness window.

questions.prompt: A report says 'accuracy 80.0%' over 5 scored cases. What is the honest thing to write instead?
options: 'Accuracy 80%, within 1% of the best model'
'The model's accuracy is at least 80%'
'The model got 4 of 5 cases right - too few to distinguish it from a model that got 3' - because at n=5 and p=0.8 the standard error is about 0.18, so the number swings wildly on one case
'Accuracy 80% (n=5)'
questions.explain: At p=0.8, n=5: sqrt(0.8*0.2/5) = sqrt(0.032) is about 0.18 - roughly 18 percentage points of standard error, so a one-case difference (20 points) is inside the noise. The honest statement names the denominator and refuses the precision. Option 2 claims a comparison the data cannot support. Option 3 attaches the n but still presents 80.0% as a stable estimate with four significant figures. Option 4 turns a point estimate into a lower bound, which the data does not license.

questions.prompt: A model has 95% accuracy but mean ECE 0.30. What is going on, and which metric matters if 0.6 is your auto-route threshold?
options: The two numbers contradict each other, so one of them is a bug
ECE only applies to choice questions, so it is meaningless here
Accuracy always beats ECE, so the model is fine

It is usually right but badly calibrated - the stated probabilities are wrong. If 0.6 is a threshold you act on, calibration matters, because the probability near the threshold is exactly what you are trusting
questions.explain: Accuracy asks whether the top answer was right; ECE asks whether the stated probability matched how often it was right. A model can be right on the label while being wildly overconfident - 95% accuracy with ECE 0.30 is the classic case. Which metric you care about depends on what the probability is FOR: if 0.6 is the auto-route threshold, then the numbers near 0.6 are deciding real work, so calibration is the metric that matters, and a reliability diagram from metrics.reliability_bins() is the tool. The two metrics are not in conflict (they answer different questions), ECE applies to noul as well as choice, and 'accuracy always wins' is false exactly when the probability is used as a threshold.

questions.prompt: What is the most useful test of whether a number in a report deserves more precision?
options: Check whether the number has two decimal places
Check whether the number is bigger than the previous run's number
Check whether the report includes a battery hash
Ask what decision you would make differently if the number were three points higher - if nothing changes, you do not need more precision
questions.explain: Interpretation is the last step and it is not the harness's job: the harness produces numbers, you decide what they mean. The decision-relevant test is what you would DO differently - 'would I ship it?' - and if the answer is the same at 80% and 83%, the precision is noise. Decimal places are cosmetic, not evidential. Being bigger than last time is not a reason (the battery hash may even differ, so you are comparing different cases). The battery hash is worth checking - but for comparability, not for precision: two reports with different hashes were measured against different questions.

questions.prompt: Connect this to the repo: you open runs/20261025-040448-mock.md and see a full report with 'scored cases 5' and 'accuracy 33.3%'. What is that file evidence OF?
options: That the mock model is bad at routing
That decision models generally score about a third on routing tickets
That the routing battery is well designed and the case count is right
That the harness runs end to end offline - metrics, groups, latency and the report all work. It is not evidence about any model, and run_report() says so in a SIMULATED RUN banner at the top
questions.explain: This is the repo's rule 4 in action: the mock is an offline simulator that exists to test the harness, and its numbers must never be published as a model evaluation. run_report() checks result.provider.startswith('mock') and prepends the banner saying so. So the file is committed evidence that the harness works - files land, the metrics compute, the report renders - and nothing else. It says nothing about real routing ability (option 3 is exactly the mistake the banner exists to prevent), and 'the mock is bad at routing' is meaningless because the mock does not route.
